re-testudo-horsfieldii.title: Russian Tortoise
re-testudo-horsfieldii.summary: A hardy, active, burrowing tortoise from Central Asia. It can live 50 years or more, so it's a long-term commitment.
rows: 5–10 in shell length. Males are smaller
One adult: 7 × 3.5 ft floor space (24.5 sq ft) minimum, or an outdoor pen when the weather allows. Juveniles under about 6 in can use 4 × 2 ft temporarily. Add 10 sq ft for each extra tortoise
Always provide a humid hide with damp substrate. Juvenile enclosures should be 40–75%
Strong UVB is required, plus bright daylight lighting. Lights on about 14 h in summer and 10 h in winter
High-fiber, low-protein, low-sugar: leafy greens, grasses and edible weeds such as dandelion and clover. Not grocery vegetables or fruit as a staple. Feed on a plate
Most dislike handling. Scoop up from below with both hands and support the body. Wash hands before and after
Active by day and loves to dig. Give 4–6 in of loose sand and soil substrate
Central Asia (dry steppe and rocky desert)
notes: Not a social species, so it's fine kept alone. Don't house males together.
warn: Lives 50+ years and needs far more floor space than most tanks provide.

re-centrochelys-sulcata.title: Sulcata Tortoise (African Spurred Tortoise)
re-centrochelys-sulcata.summary: The largest mainland tortoise and third-largest tortoise in the world, from the southern edge of the Sahara. Cute hatchlings grow fast into 70–110 lb diggers that need a large, secure outdoor pen and can live 70+ years.
rows: Usually 24–30 in (61–76 cm) and 70–110 lb as adults; big males can pass 40 in and 200 lb
Juveniles under 10 in: 7 × 3.5 × 2.5 ft (24.5 sq ft) minimum indoors. Adults need a pen of about 20 × 10 ft (300 sq ft) or more, realistically outdoors, with strong walls sunk 12 in into the ground
Basking 100–105°F, ambient/cool 80–90°F, night 70–75°F. Outdoors, give heated shelter if nights fall below 50°F
Juveniles need high humidity (over 80%, e.g. in a humid burrow/hide) to avoid dehydration; adults are more tolerant
Strong UVB indoors (UVI 4.0–6.0 at the basking area); natural sun outdoors
Herbivore: grasses, weeds and greens (e.g. Bermuda grass) with variety. Juveniles as much as they eat daily; near adulthood about a shell-sized portion daily to prevent obesity
Active by day; strong digger and burrower
Southern Sahara and the Sahel, Senegal and Mauritania east to Sudan, Eritrea and Ethiopia
notes: Avoid housing males together; males and females together will produce eggs.
Listed as endangered in the wild.
warn: Grows to 70–110+ lb, lives 70+ years and needs a large outdoor pen.

re-malacochersus-tornieri.title: Pancake Tortoise
re-malacochersus-tornieri.summary: A small East African tortoise with a remarkably flat, flexible shell that lets it wedge into rock crevices instead of hiding in its shell. Curious and agile, it can live 35 years or more.
rows: Up to about 35 years or more
One adult: 56 × 28 × 24 in (about 11 sq ft) minimum; young or small adults under 6 in can use 4 × 2 × 2 ft. Outdoors when the weather allows; add rock piles to climb and wedge into
Basking 100–108°F, cool zone 75–85°F, nights above 68°F. Bring indoors when nights fall below 58°F
Adults: no set target, but offer a humid burrow/hide. Juveniles under 4 in: 50–60% by day and up to 80% at night
Strong UVB indoors (UVI 4.0–6.0 at the basking area)
Herbivore and grazer: high-fiber grasses and weeds (e.g. Bermuda and timothy grass) rather than mainly leafy greens
Active by day; climbs rocks surprisingly well
Kenya and Tanzania (small populations in northern Zambia): rocky hillsides in dry savanna and scrub
notes: Avoid housing males together; males and females together will produce eggs.

re-chelonoidis-carbonarius.title: Red-Footed Tortoise
re-chelonoidis-carbonarius.summary: A medium-sized, omnivorous, tropical tortoise from Central and South America with red or orange scales on its legs and head. It needs warmth, high humidity, lots of floor space and a varied diet that includes fruit and some protein. It can live 50+ years.
rows: Usually 12–18 in (30–46 cm); up to 24 in is possible
Closed (not open-top) enclosure of about 8–12 × 4–6 ft floor space (32–72 sq ft) minimum, or an outdoor pen when the weather allows
Basking 90–95°F, ambient/cool 75–85°F, night 68–75°F. Bring indoors if winter days are below 65°F
70–90% (brief spikes to 100% are fine); mist 2–3× daily and always provide a humid hide
UVB indoors at UVI 2.0–3.0 in the basking area
Omnivore: about 55% fruits, flowers and leaves; 35% grasses and vegetables; 10% protein and mushrooms. Juveniles daily, adults about every other day. Calcium supplement and a cuttlebone
Active by day; forages on the forest floor
Southern Central America and northern South America east of the Andes (rainforest to savanna)

re-stigmochelys-pardalis.title: Leopard Tortoise
re-stigmochelys-pardalis.summary: A large, handsomely spotted grazing tortoise from the savannas of eastern and southern Africa. It needs lots of room (ideally an outdoor pen), strong light and UVB, dry conditions and a high-fiber diet, and it can live for many decades.
rows: Usually 40–60 cm (16–24 in) shell length and 10–20 kg; some populations reach 70 cm and 30+ kg. The commonly kept S. p. babcocki is the smaller form
Juveniles up to 15–20 cm: open tortoise table at least 100 × 60 cm (no glass tanks). Adults: 200 × 100 cm indoors is an absolute minimum; an outdoor pen of 6–10 m² or more is practically necessary
Basking surface 45–50°C (113–122°F), warm side 28–32°C (82–90°F), cool side 20–24°C (68–75°F), night 18–22°C (not below 15°C / 59°F). Does not hibernate
Low: 30–50% for adults; hatchlings 50–60% with a damp hide
High UVB: T5 HO 10–12% (about UVI 3–4 at shell height) or a mercury vapor bulb; direct sunshine is best
Strict herbivore and grazer: grasses, hay and weeds such as dandelion, plantain and clover. High fiber, low protein, low sugar; no fruit as a staple. Cuttlebone for calcium
Active by day; spends much of the day basking and grazing; likes to dig
Savannas of eastern and southern Africa, from Sudan to South Africa
warn: Grows to 16–24 in and can live 50–100 years; plan for a large outdoor pen.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Leopard tortoise care guide

re-testudo-hermanni.title: Hermann's Tortoise
re-testudo-hermanni.summary: A small-to-medium Mediterranean tortoise from southern Europe and the Balkans. Active and long-lived, it does best outdoors in a secure, sunny pen in the warm months, eats mostly weeds and leafy plants, and naturally hibernates in winter.
rows: Usually 15–25 cm (6–10 in) shell length; females are often larger

Outdoors in warm months is best: 2–3 m² minimum for one adult (4 m²+ is better), escape-proof and with sun and shade. Indoors use an open tortoise table (90 × 60 cm for hatchlings; 120 × 60 to 150 × 75 cm for larger juveniles), not a glass tank
Basking about 32–35°C (90–95°F), warm zone 26–30°C, cool zone 20–24°C, night usually 16–20°C
Provide slightly humid shelters (and short lukewarm soaks for juveniles)
UVB essential indoors: mercury vapor bulb or T5 HO 10–12% tube (about UVI 3–4 at shell height); natural sun outdoors
Mainly herbivore: low-protein, high-fiber weeds and leafy plants (e.g. chickweed, dandelion); calcium supplement
Active by day; digs, grazes and basks
Southern Europe (Spain, France, Italy) and the Balkans
notes: Males often harass females or other males and may need to be housed separately.
In the wild it hibernates through mild to cool winters; only hibernate a healthy, well-prepared tortoise.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Hermann's tortoise care guide

re-indotestudo-elongata.title: Elongated Tortoise
re-indotestudo-elongata.summary: A medium-sized forest tortoise from South and Southeast Asia with a long, blotchy yellow-brown shell; adults often develop pink around the nose and eyes. It's an omnivore that needs warmth, humid retreats and lots of floor space, and it isn't a good first tortoise.
rows: Usually 28–30 cm (11–12 in) shell length; up to 36 cm
About 275 × 140 cm (9 × 4.5 ft) for one animal; larger is better. A warm forest-floor pen with cover, retreats and a soaking pool
Ambient 24–29°C (75–84°F), basking 30–32°C (86–90°F), shaded retreat 22–24°C, night 18–22°C. Do not hibernate
UVB needed indoors at moderate strength (about UVI 1–2 at shell height); 10–12 hour light cycle
Omnivore: varied leaves, weeds, flowers and fungi, some fruit and occasional animal matter
Most active in the rainy season; shelters through hot or dry spells
Nepal and northern/eastern India through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam to southern China and northern Malaysia
notes: House males separately; solitary housing is the safer default.
Critically endangered in the wild; buy only documented captive-bred animals.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Elongated tortoise care guide

re-geochelone-elegans.title: Indian Star Tortoise
re-geochelone-elegans.summary: A medium-sized Asian tortoise famous for the radiating yellow star pattern on each shell scute. It needs warmth year-round (no hibernation), strong light and UVB, clean dry footing with a humid retreat, and a fiber-rich plant diet. Not a casual beginner tortoise.
rows: Around 20–30 cm (8–12 in) shell length; females are usually larger
Hatchlings: indoor table about 90 × 60 cm. One adult: 2 × 1 m indoors is only a cold-weather minimum; an outdoor pen of 4–6 m² or more in warm weather
Basking about 32–35°C (90–95°F), warm zone 27–30°C, cooler area 24–26°C, night best above about 22°C (72°F). Does not hibernate
Adults about 50–70% with a more humid retreat; hatchlings and juveniles benefit from a humid hide at 70–80%
Strong UVB indoors (about UVI 3–4 at shell height, e.g. a T5 HO 10–12% tube); natural sun when safe
Keep handling minimal; lift with two hands under the plastron, close to the ground
Active by day; walks, grazes and basks
India, Sri Lanka and Pakistan (dry scrub and grassland)
notes: House singly unless the pen is large with duplicate basking and feeding spots; males may chase and ram.
International trade is tightly restricted (CITES); buy only documented captive-bred animals.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Indian star tortoise care guide

re-chelonoidis-denticulatus.title: Yellow-Footed Tortoise
re-chelonoidis-denticulatus.summary: A large South American rainforest tortoise with yellow-to-orange scales on its head and legs. It's bigger and more tied to warm, humid forest than its cousin the red-footed tortoise, eats a varied omnivorous diet, and can live 50–70 years.
rows: About 14 in for most animals, but some populations reach 16–24 in (40–60 cm) or more and 7–20 kg
One adult needs at least about 6 m² (65 sq ft) of indoor floor space; 8–12 m² is better. Heated, humid house even if it uses an outdoor pen in warm weather
Daytime air 25–28°C (77–82°F), broad basking patch 30–32°C, shaded retreat 23–25°C, night 22–24°C. Avoid long periods below 22°C. Do not hibernate
About 75–90% with airflow, drainage and some dry surfaces; always a shallow soaking basin
Bright light plus moderate UVB (about UVI 1–2 at shell height); 11–13 hours a day
Omnivore: varied leaves, weeds, flowers and mushrooms, limited fruit, and occasional invertebrate protein (e.g. earthworms or snails)
Active by day on the forest floor
Tropical South America east of the Andes (Amazon and Guiana regions) and Trinidad
notes: House singly unless the enclosure is exceptionally large; males fight.

sources.name: Herpeton Academy – Yellow-footed tortoise care guide
Reptiles Magazine – Yellow-footed tortoise care sheet
